article_text:
The Museum of Contemporary Art Antwerp (M HKA) in Belgium is recruiting an Artistic Director and an Executive Director as it introduces a shared leadership model to guide its artistic, institutional and strategic development.

Open Call:

The Museum of Contemporary Art Antwerp (M HKA) has announced two senior leadership vacancies as part of a new management structure built around shared responsibility. The museum is seeking an Artistic Director and an Executive Director who will work together as a unified leadership team, jointly responsible for determining the institution’s future direction. The Artistic Director will oversee artistic strategy, the museum’s collection and its programme, while the Executive Director will be responsible for organisational management, financial sustainability and staffing.

The appointments follow the museum board’s July 2026 decision to strengthen M HKA’s position as an artistically ambitious, collection-centred institution, with collaboration and professional networks central to its development.

Institutional Context :

Founded in 1987, M HKA is a contemporary art museum in Antwerp, Belgium, with an internationally recognised collection and an established role in the Flemish and European cultural landscape. As a founding member of L’Internationale, a European confederation of museums, the institution remains committed to international artistic exchange and collaboration. The recruitment comes amid an institutional transition. In October 2025, plans for the museum’s new building were cancelled, while proposed reforms to the Flemish museum sector raised questions about its institutional status. Following opposition from the arts sector, the decision concerning its museum status was reversed.

M HKA is now undertaking a transition process extending to 2028, to secure its long-term artistic and organisational sustainability. In 2027, the museum will celebrate its fortieth anniversary through a programme developed with partners across the cultural sector.

Eligibility and Criteria :

The museum is recruiting for two distinct leadership positions:

Artistic Director : The appointed candidate will lead the museum’s artistic direction, collection strategy and programming, working collaboratively with the Executive Director to establish the institution’s long-term priorities.

Executive Director : The appointed candidate will oversee the museum’s organisational, financial and staffing responsibilities, ensuring the institutional structures necessary to support its artistic ambitions.

Both positions require a commitment to shared leadership and collaboration.

The museum’s announcement does not provide specific qualifications, professional experience requirements, or language criteria. Applicants should consult the individual vacancy descriptions for the complete eligibility requirements.

Evaluation Process:

Applications will undergo an assessment process followed by interviews with a selection committee. The museum’s Governing Body will make the final appointment decisions by the end of 2026. The successful candidates are expected to assume their positions in spring 2027. The two directors will jointly develop M HKA’s strategic plan for 2029 to 2034, which must be submitted to the Flemish government in 2028 as part of the institution’s application for structural funding.

Practical Information:

Application deadline: 1 November 2026

Institution: Museum of Contemporary Art Antwerp (M HKA)

Location: Antwerp, Belgium

Available positions: Artistic Director and Executive Director

Selection decision: By the end of 2026

Expected commencement: Spring 2027

Strategic planning period: 2029 to 2034

The appointments form part of M HKA’s institutional transition, which is scheduled to continue until 2028.

The announcement does not specify salary, contract duration, working arrangements, or other employment conditions; these should be confirmed through the individual vacancy listings.

Applications and Queries:

Applications for both positions are open until 1 November 2026 .

Candidates should consult M HKA’s official recruitment platform for the full job descriptions, eligibility requirements, application procedures and supporting documentation.

Apply here: https://muhka-jobs.cvw.io/

Further information: https://www.muhka.be/en/m-hka-embeds-shared-leadership-in-new-management-structure/

Applicants are encouraged to review the requirements for their chosen position before applying.

article_text:
On Friday, Art Week NYC , a four-day event taking place throughout the city from November 11 through 14, announced a list of 32 participating institutions. They include museums like the Whitney Museum of American Art, the Studio Museum in Harlem, and the Queens Museum; nonprofits like ArtTable, the Madison Square Park Conservancy, and the Brooklyn Experimental Art Foundation; and many other citywide arts organizations.

ARTnews , along with sister publication Art in America and Artforum , three of the leading authorities on contemporary art, launched Art Week NYC earlier this summer. The event promises to bring together galleries, museums, artists, collectors, cultural organizations, and audiences over four days of programming, from walking tours to artist talks to gallery openings. Art Week NYC is centered around the city’s four main gallery neighborhoods: Chelsea, the Lower East Side, Tribeca, and the Upper East Side.

“New York City’s world-renowned galleries and museums draw art lovers from all over the globe, but they belong first and foremost to the New Yorkers who live here,” said City Council Speaker Julie Menin about Art Week NYC. “Art Week NYC opens the door for our city’s own artists and art lovers to support and be inspired by the creative institutions in our own backyard. The success of our city’s cultural sphere has always been built on the voices and hearts of New Yorkers, and this week gives more of them a way to take part.”

On Saturday, November 14, there will be a full day of public programming at the New Museum, Art Week NYC’s main institutional partner. (The New Museum, along with select other institutions, are presented in partnership with Bloomberg Connects.) Artforum ’s series of five talks, titled “Art and the City,” will take place in the New Museum’s theater and will feature artists, architects, filmmakers, critics, and writers in conversation over the course of the day. Topics will include the redesign of notable museum spaces across the city, the growing movement of artists into filmmaking, the economic conditions faced by artists working in New York, and the impact of machine intelligence on studio practice.

"是的，我在那里跟着谢尔盖·索洛维约夫学习电影和戏剧。我不知道他现在是否知名，但他曾是俄罗斯电影的一代宗师。他和费里尼、安东尼奥尼这样的人都是朋友。在俄罗斯，戏剧学校的学习是连轴转的：我们几乎就住在学校里！当我遇到索洛维约夫时，我立刻就爱上了他，因为他是个真正的朋克。他告诉我们：“我爱你们本来的样子，所以保持本色吧，别装什么好学生！”这卸下了我心头的一块大石。我觉得自己被允许去感受事物，去感受自己的身体。我改变了看电影的方式，结识了新朋友，改变了穿衣风格……一切都变了！他在我身上看到了连我自己都没有意识到的东西。如果没遇到他，我都不知道自己现在会在哪里。", "我很年轻的时候就看过他的一部电影，可能是《回归》[注：他的首部长片，荣获2003年威尼斯电影节金狮奖，讲述了两兄弟面对一个他们从未见过的父亲神秘回归的故事。自俄罗斯入侵乌克兰以来，这位导演已在欧洲流亡多年，编者按]，但我无论如何都记得自己当时被迷住了。我从未看过可以称之为艺术电影、氛围电影的作品。我曾梦想与安德烈合作，但脑海中有一个声音告诉我这是不可能的，我和他之间的差距太大了。当我走进试镜房间的那一秒，这个声音就消失了，当时他和他的联合编剧西蒙·利亚琴科正站在那里。他一直以平等的方式与我对话。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "您为这个角色做了哪些准备？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "安德烈不喜欢过度心理化、什么都想刨根问底的演员。我则是从自身出发去契合加林娜的情感状态，比如通过音乐。为了表达她的绝望，安德烈给我描绘了一个震颤线条突然变细或消失的意象。这非常相似。我不想思考太多，以便与我的身体保持贴近。此外，安德烈还让我们自由发挥。拍摄时，台词说完后他并没有喊停：他要求我们把场景延续下去，在里面生活。加林娜在夜里阳台上情绪爆发的那场戏，剧本里写的是不到1分钟。其余的全是即兴发挥。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在接受《Flanelle Magazine》采访时，据说您和饰演格列布的德米特里·马祖罗夫在片场曾因对角色动机意见不合而争吵。这挺有意思的……", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在试镜时，我试图向德米特里解释我认为他们这对伴侣出了什么问题。他对我说：“她什么都有，有漂亮的房子、有钱……她还想要什么？”这让我气疯了！我们在试镜现场吵了起来，当我转向安德烈和西蒙时，他们正咧着嘴笑。在片场又发生了一次这种情况，但安德烈拒绝判定我们谁对谁错。读了德米特里的采访后，我明白我们只是对现状持有两种截然相反的观点。许多男性大概会和他有同感，但我能理解加林娜感到的那种空虚。最重要的是，我明白安德烈选角眼光极佳。（笑。）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "安德烈·兹维亚金采夫曾告诉我们，他想从夏布洛尔的原著中拍出一部“深刻的俄罗斯”电影。除了乌克兰战争的背景，您认为是什么让《弥诺陶洛斯》成为一部俄罗斯电影？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是一个难题。有人告诉我，俄罗斯人民经历过很多苦难，这在他们的文学作品中随处可见，苦难无处不在。但我发现世界各地的观众都能对这部电影产生共鸣。也许父权制的压力更大一些，因为在俄罗斯，女性结婚后放弃职业是再正常不过的事。我一直觉得加林娜觉得自己被这种处境困住了。从内心来讲，她是一个死去的女人。她不再为自己而活了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在俄罗斯，您是否听到过关于这部电影及其在戛纳获奖的反响？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我不再住在俄罗斯了，但人们写信告诉我他们对看这部电影的兴奋心情……或者说想方设法去观看它。还有一些人对安德烈非常愤怒，尽管他们很可能永远也不会看到《弥诺陶洛斯》。对于这些人，我建议他们去看一看，然后形成自己的见解。一部伟大的电影的力量就在于引发对话，提出更多的问题，而不是给出现成的答案。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "最后，您最喜欢的3部俄罗斯电影是什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我给您列出脑海中立刻浮现的三部：马连·胡齐耶夫的《我二十岁》（1965）、谢尔盖·索洛维约夫的《阿萨》（1987）以及安德烈·兹维亚金采夫的《利维坦》（2014）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", C’est assez amusant…"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Lors des auditions, j’essayais d’expliquer à Dmitri ce qui, selon moi, n’allait pas dans leur couple. Il m’a dit : « Elle a tout, une belle maison, de l’argent… qu’est-ce qu’elle veut de plus ? » Cela m’a rendue folle ! Nous nous sommes disputés en salle de casting et, quand je me suis tournée vers Andreï et Simon, ils faisaient un grand sourire. C’est arrivé une seconde fois sur le tournage, mais Andreï refusait de donner raison à l’un d’entre nous. Hormis le contexte de la guerre en Ukraine, selon vous, qu’est-ce qui fait de Minotaure un film russe ?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "C’est une question difficile. Quelqu’un m’a dit que le peuple russe a beaucoup souffert et qu’on le retrouve dans sa littérature, où la souffrance est omniprésente. article_text:
Vous avez étudié à la prestigieuse école de cinéma VGIK de Moscou. Quel souvenir en gardez-vous ?

Oui, j’y ai étudié le cinéma et le théâtre avec Sergueï Soloviov. Je ne sais pas s’il est connu aujourd’hui, mais c’était un grand maître du cinéma russe. Il était ami avec des gens comme Fellini et Antonioni. En Russie, dans les écoles de théâtre, c’est du non-stop : on vit presque sur place ! Quand j’ai rencontré Soloviov, je l’ai tout de suite adoré car c’était un vrai punk. Il nous disait : « Je vous aime tels que vous êtes, alors restez vous-mêmes, ne jouez pas les bons élèves ! » Cela m’a libérée d’un poids. Je me suis sentie autorisée à ressentir les choses, à ressentir mon corps. J’ai changé ma manière de voir les films, j’ai fréquenté de nouvelles personnes, je me suis habillée différemment… tout a changé ! Il voyait quelque chose en moi dont je n’avais pas conscience. Je ne sais pas où je serais si je ne l’avais pas rencontré.

Vous avez découvert les films d’Andreï Zviaguintsev lors de vos années étudiantes. Que vous inspirait son œuvre avant de travailler avec lui ?

J’ai vu un de ses films quand j’étais encore jeune, c’était peut-être Le Retour [son premier long-métrage, Lion d’or à la Mostra de Venise 2003, qui voit deux frères confrontés au retour mystérieux d’un père qu’ils n’ont jamais connu. Le cinéaste s’est exilé en Europe depuis plusieurs années, dans le sillage de l’invasion russe en Ukraine, ndlr] mais je me souviens en tout cas d’avoir été hypnotisée. Je n’avais jamais vu ce qu’on pourrait appeler un film d’art, un film d’atmosphère. Je rêvais de travailler avec Andreï, mais une voix dans ma tête me disait que c’était impossible, que l’écart entre lui et moi était trop grand. Cette voix s’est évanouie à la seconde où je suis entrée dans la salle de casting, où il se tenait avec son coscénariste Simon Liachenko. Il s’est toujours adressé à moi d’égal à égal.

En quoi votre préparation pour le rôle a-t-elle consisté ?

Andreï n’aime pas les acteurs qui psychologisent trop, qui veulent tout savoir. J’ai cherché de mon côté à embrasser l’état émotionnel de Galina, par exemple à travers la musique. Pour exprimer son désespoir, Andreï m’a donné l’image d’une ligne de vibration qui soudain s’étiole ou disparaît. C’est très similaire. Je n’avais pas envie de trop réfléchir pour rester proche de mon corps. Andreï nous a d’ailleurs laissé improviser. Lorsqu’on tournait, une fois les dialogues prononcés, il ne coupait pas : il nous demandait de prolonger la scène, de vivre à l’intérieur. Celle où Galina implose au balcon, la nuit, durait moins d’une minute dans le script. Tout le reste a été improvisé.

Dans un entretien pour Flanelle Magazine, on peut lire que vous et Dmitri Mazourov, qui joue Gleb, vous disputiez sur le tournage car vous n’étiez pas d’accord quant aux motivations de votre personnage. C’est assez amusant…

Lors des auditions, j’essayais d’expliquer à Dmitri ce qui, selon moi, n’allait pas dans leur couple. Il m’a dit : « Elle a tout, une belle maison, de l’argent… qu’est-ce qu’elle veut de plus ? » Cela m’a rendue folle ! Nous nous sommes disputés en salle de casting et, quand je me suis tournée vers Andreï et Simon, ils faisaient un grand sourire. C’est arrivé une seconde fois sur le tournage, mais Andreï refusait de donner raison à l’un d’entre nous. En lisant les interviews de Dmitri, j’ai compris qu’on avait juste deux points de vue opposés sur la situation. Beaucoup d’hommes penseront sans doute comme lui, mais moi, je comprends ce vide que ressent Galina. Et je comprends surtout qu’Andreï a bien choisi son casting. (Rires.)

Andreï Zviaguintsev nous a déclaré qu’il avait voulu tirer un film « profondément russe » de l’œuvre originale de Chabrol. Hormis le contexte de la guerre en Ukraine, selon vous, qu’est-ce qui fait de Minotaure un film russe ?

C’est une question difficile. Quelqu’un m’a dit que le peuple russe a beaucoup souffert et qu’on le retrouve dans sa littérature, où la souffrance est omniprésente. Mais je me rends compte que les spectateurs s’approprient le film partout dans le monde. Peut-être que les enjeux patriarcaux sont plus forts, car en Russie c’est tout à fait normal qu’une femme abandonne son métier une fois qu’elle s’est mariée. Je me suis toujours dit que Galina se sentait piégée par cette situation. À l’intérieur, c’est une femme morte. Elle ne vit plus pour elle-même.

Avez-vous eu des échos sur la réception du film et de son prix à Cannes en Russie ?

Je ne vis plus en Russie, mais les gens m’écrivent pour me dire leur excitation à l’idée de voir le film… ou de trouver un moyen de le voir. D’autres sont très remontés contre Andreï, alors même qu’ils ne verront sans doute jamais Minotaure . À ceux-là, je leur conseille de le voir et de se forger leur propre opinion. C’est le pouvoir d’un grand film que d’inviter à la conversation, de poser davantage de questions qu’il ne donne de réponses toutes faites.

Pour finir, quels sont vos trois films russes préférés ?

Je vous cite les trois qui me viennent instantanément : J’ai vingt ans de Marlen Khoutsiev (1965), Assa de Sergueï Soloviov (1987) et Léviathan d’Andreï Zviaguintsev (2014).

article_text:
Jamie Dornan , who is set to star as Aragorn in “ Lord of the Rings : The Hunt for Gollum,” is getting candid about what it means to step into the role originated by Viggo Mortensen for the forthcoming installment of the beloved franchise.

“I cried. I actually cried,” Dornan told Entertainment Tonight when asked how he reacted to the news of his casting. “It’s like a dream. It’s an absolute dream and an honor to be entering that world in any capacity, let alone playing a character of such significance and such admiration, and that we all love and love what Viggo did with that role in those three films.”

He continued, noting that filming “The Hunt for Gollum” was “incredible.” “[I’m] incredibly honored and had a brilliant time. I finished like three weeks ago. It was an incredible experience, and I hope people welcome our story into that world because a lot of people care about it, and I really realize that. But yeah, hopefully we’ve done a good job of it.”

Last month, Dornan admitted during an interview with L’Officiel that while there is “pressure” on him to live up to Mortensen’s take on the character, there’s no part of him that is “trying to outdo him.” “I’ve been asked to play a super iconic role, and I’ll do my best. But for me, Aragorn will always be just Viggo. His performance is one of my all-time favorites, and I feel honored to try to recapture at least some of the energy he originally brought to the character,” he said.

The ensemble also sees the return of Ian McKellen (as Gandalf), Elijah Wood (Frodo) and Lee Pace (King Thranduil), in addition to new cast members Kate Winslet (Marigol), Leo Woodall (Halvard) and Anya Taylor-Joy as an elf.

Patrick Stewart, who died Wednesday at 86 , starred in dozens of film, shows and TV movies across 60 years on screen. He was best known for playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard on “Star Trek” and Prof. Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” movies, and he received four Emmy nominations, three Golden Globe noms, a Tony nod and one Grammy win during his career.

“His professional accomplishments were humbly matched by his philanthropy and activism on behalf of human rights, survivors of domestic violence, global refugees, veterans’ mental health services, and animal welfare, particularly his cherished foster pitties,” a statement on his Instagram read. “He was a Knight, Chancellor, motor sport enthusiast, and lifelong Huddersfield Football fan. He will be remembered for the dignity, compassion and humanity he brought to every role — in his art and life.”

Stewart’s “Star Trek” and Marvel co-stars have shared tributes to him online, in addition to his countless fans.

“Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor,” wrote fellow “Star Trek” icon William Shatner. “From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work. My heart goes out to Sunny and his family. He will be deeply missed.”

Revisit Stewart’s career in photos below.

Dune (1984) Image Credit: ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection In David Lynch’s 1984 version of “Dune,” Stewart played Gurney Halleck, a troubador-warrior and baliset musician in the Atreides court, co-starring with Kyle MacLachlan and Max Von Sydow.

Star Trek: The Next Generation (1987) Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Col Stewart debuted as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, the commanding officer of the Federation starship USS Enterprise, when “Star Trek: The Next Generation” aired on September 28, 1987.

Star Trek: Generations (1994) Stewart reprised his role as Picard on the big screen in “Star Trek: Generations” on November 18, 1994. He starred in later “Star Trek” movies like “First Contact” (1996), “Insurrection” (1998) and “Nemesis” (2002).

Moby Dick (1998) Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection As Captain Ahab, Stewart hunted down the great white whale that had bitten off his leg years prior in this TV mini-series adaptation of Herman Melville’s novel. He was nominated for an Emmy for the role.

Safe House (1998) Image Credit: ©Showtime Networks Inc./Courtes Stewart played Mace Sowell, a retired DIA agent that has incriminating evidence on his former boss who’s now running for president. The TV film aired in the UK in late 1998 and in the U.S. in January 1999.

A Christmas Carol (1999) Image Credit: ©Hallmark Entertainment/Courtes As Ebenezer Scrooge, Stewart was visited by the Ghosts of Christmas Past, Present and Yet to Come in this holiday TV movie.

X-Men (2000) Image Credit: ©20thCentFox/Courtesy Everett C Stewart debuted as Prof. Charles Xavier, the leader of the X-Men mutant team, in the 2000 film. His powerful telekinetic mutant mentored young heroes and clashed with his old friend and rival Magneto (Ian McKellen). He also appeared in sequels and spinoffs like “X2” (2003), “The Last Stand” (2006), “X-Men Origins: Wolverine” (2009), “The Wolverine” (2013) and “Days of Future Past” (2014).

King of Texas (2002) Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection This TV film reinvented Shakespeare’s “King Lear” and set the tale in the Republic of Texas during the 19th century. Stewart starred as John Lear, a wealthy cattle baron who divided his land amongst his daughters.

The Lion in Winter (2003) Image Credit: ©Showtime Networks Inc./Courtes Stewart played King Henry II in this TV film, which co-starred Glenn Close as Eleanor of Aquitaine. He was nominated for a Golden Globe for his role in this TV movie remake of the Peter O’Toole classic.

Green Room (2015) Image Credit: Everett Collection / Everett Collection In Jeremy Saulnier’s thriller, Stewart plays the bar owner and leader of a Nazi group who attack a punk band that has just witnessed a murder in the Pacific Northwest.

Blunt Talk (2015) Image Credit: ©Starz! Movie Channel/Courtesy In this Starz series, Stewart played Walter Blunt, a military veteran and turned cable journalist, and received another Golden Globe nomination.

Logan (2017) Image Credit: ©20thCentFox/Courtesy Everett Collection Stewart and Hugh Jackman reunited as Xavier and Wolverine in “Logan,” the first R-rated “X-Men” spinoff. In the future-set spinoff, Xavier suffered from a degenerative disease and accidentally killed many mutants, and his character dies in the film alongside Wolverine.

Avengers: Doomsday (2026) In what may be his final on-screen appearance, Stewart will return as Xavier in “Avengers: Doomsday” on Dec. 18. It will mark the first time that the Avengers, X-Men, Fantastic Four and more heroes will all cross over in the MCU.

article_text:
Pocket Review

This Iranian Documentary Wasn’t Meant to Begin This Way

In Mani Haghighi’s new film, an artist’s extensive archive draws the ire of the authorities.

I Deserve a Lover Whose Every Rise Sets Fiery Dooms Raging Across the Skies (2026) poster (all images courtesy Film at Lincoln Center)

Mani Haghighi’s documentary, I Deserve a Lover Whose Every Rise Sets Fiery Dooms Raging Across the Skies (2026), opens with a diverse group of stone-faced archivists in a beautiful, jewel-toned room lined with books and ephemera. They suit up in masks and gloves to root through garbage bags filled with photo albums, broken pottery, and other artifacts of unknown provenance, caked in dirt and debris. However, as the Iranian director’s voice-over narration explains, “This film wasn’t meant to begin this way.” Authorities confiscated the footage Haghighi shot for the original opening, “a girl standing on a foggy mountain road, searching for a phone signal,” when they raided the film crew’s hotel room in Tabriz. Their crime was depicting a woman without a headscarf.

I Deserve a Lover Whose Every Rise Sets Fiery Dooms Raging Across the Skies is a document of documentation — of discovery, preservation, and remembrance. Haghighi focuses on Iranian artist Nasser Bakhshi and his wife, Roghayeh Najdi, and their monumental archive of cultural history, from the pre-Islamic era to the Iranian Revolution and into today, arranged in their home. Bakhshi and Najdi are charming, eccentrically stylish, and in love. They are beloved by the Persian rug dealers whom Haghighi interviews about the couple’s intense shopping habit. Haghighi asks aloud whether Bakhshi is a hoarder, and the artist responds, “I collect consciously, methodically, and logically … I’m aware of my instinct.”

article_text:
Kenny Ortega is the talent behind iconic films ranging from “Hocus Pocus” to “High School Musical” not to mention dozens of music videos, concerts and two Olympics opening ceremonies. So it’s unsurprising he was the top choice when Lego were thinking about making their first musical feature based on the Lego Friends line.

Ortega, who says Lego has been “part of my life for over 30 years,” was brought on to executive produce “Lego Friends: Heartlake the Musical,” shaping the story and choreography as well as picking the director (his longtime collaborator Paul Becker), location (London, U.K.) and actors. He calls the all-British cast “triple threats” who could sing, dance and act, saying they reminded him of working with a 15-year-old Christian Bale on “Newsies.”

The 50-minute film, which is set to premiere Oct. 16 on Lego’s YouTube channel, as well as Peacock and Netflix, follows a young girl, Daisy (Jada Langley) as she is magically transported into the world of Heartlake City where she makes some fast friends and helps them save a special landmark.

Popular on Variety

Ahead of the film’s launch, Ortega sat down with Variety to talk about how he ended up working on the project, whether he has ideas for a sequel and his plans for the L.A. Olympics.

Hanah Draper and Michael McKenna [from production company Final Pixel] reached out to me and said, “Do you like Lego?” I was like, “Lego’s been part of my life for over 30 years.” I’ve got a nephew — every birthday, every holiday, every special occasion [it’s] Lego, Lego, Lego. I was like, “We love Legos!” So it was easy for me to say, “I’d love to take a meeting, I’d love to hear more about it,” and that’s how it began.

Final Pixel is an award-winning global creative virtual production innovation studio and so the way they pitched it to me was [they would] basically create a 3D virtual world that we would build sets in front of and on this giant curved LED screen. And that right away was it for me. Because I mean, I’ve been making films since virtual reality didn’t exist. Visual effects were painted on glass, or you know, wire removal, and so this was an opportunity for me as a producer and storyteller to work in a capacity that I hadn’t before, and that really excited me.

Oh yeah. I was brought in primarily in the beginning as an executive producer to develop the story and help the writers come to understand how music, song and dance production can move character and story forward in the storytelling of our movie.

My work skews older than what this project set out to accomplish. Where the Lego Friends universe is like, six years-old and up, mine is a little older than that with Disney, with “High School Musical” and “Descendants,” “Cheetah Girls,” and “Julie and the Phantoms” at Netflix, and so I thought that’s what they wanted. So in the beginning I would say what changed was that I had to sort of age down, and to put on a new thinking cap and to go, “Okay, I’m now creating something for maybe five years-old.” So that was fun, that was different, that was unique.

We came back and did a few reshoots, so the total, I would say maybe — under 30 days? Like 25, 26, days.

We had a lot of fun, deciding on how to build Heartlake, what to incorporate in it, what characters would take on the main roles in a first little musical. I mean, this was all a test. We came at it with a modest amount of money and time because they had never done it, and this was an experiment, sort of. Let’s see what we can accomplish here, and then maybe this gives us an opportunity to go bigger and beyond this, and I hope that that will be the story.

Heck yeah! It was a lot of fun.

I’m not. I’m so excited about it though, I hope to be invited to opening and closing ceremonies. I want to get tickets to see the events. I was an athlete growing up. My father was an Olympic athlete, track and field athlete. I have not been invited. I don’t even know who is creatively going to be running that aspect of the Olympics, the ceremonies. But it was the time of my life working with Don Mischer and Mitt Romney in Salt Lake and the folks in Atlanta for the Summer Games and I would love to at least be there to witness what comes to Los Angeles.

Richard Riehle , an actor in Office Space , Bridesmaids , Casino , Deuce Bigalow: Male Gigolo and The Man From Earth , has died. He was 78.

Riehle played Tom Smykowski, a cynical Initech product manager, in Mike Judge’s 1999 satirical comedy Office Space , sharing credits with Ron Livingston, Jennifer Aniston, Stephen Root and Gary Cole.

“We are deeply saddened to confirm the passing of our beloved client, Richard Riehle, this past weekend,” Riehle’s reps said in a statement to Deadline .

The statement continued, “A remarkable actor whose career in theater, film, and television spanned nearly five decades and more than 400 projects, Richard leaves behind an extraordinary legacy. Beyond his immense talent, he will be remembered for his genuine goodness, boundless kindness, and unwavering generosity, particularly toward emerging actors and filmmakers, whom he encouraged and supported at every opportunity. Our industry has lost an exceptional talent, and our community has lost a truly wonderful man. We ask that his family’s privacy be respected during this difficult time.”

Riehle was born on May 12, 1948, in Menomonee Falls, WI. He first entered the entertainment industry in the John Wayne-starring western Rooster Cogburn in 1975.

Other film credits include Joyride (1977), Black Rain (1989), Of Mice and Men (1992), Free Willy (1993), The Fugitive (1993), Lightning Jack (1994), Casino (1995), Ghosts of Mississippi (1996), The Odd Couple II (1998), Lethal Weapon 4 (1998), Office Space (1999), Deuce Bigalo: Make Gigolo (1999), Joe Dirt (2001), Beethoven’s 5th (2003), Wedding Crashers (2005), National Lampoon’s Dom Daze 2 (2006), Red (2008), Halloween II (2009), Bridesmaids (2011), A Very Harold & Kumar 3D Christmas (2011), Texas Chainsaw 3D (2013), Lovesick (2014). His last film credit was in 2026, in The Cowboy Killer .

On television, Riehle first appeared in the TV film The Other Side of Hell . The actor would go on to appear in My Two Dads (1989), Dragnet (1989) and Falcon Crest (1989).

Other TV shows in which Riehle appears include Quantum Leap , Murder, Show Wrote , L.A. Law , Ferris Bueller , The Golden Girls , Roseanne , Star Trek: The Next Generation , Ally McBeal , The Practice , Buffy the Vampire Slayer , Chicago Hope , Home Improvement , Columbo , Star Trek: Voyager , Sabrina, the Teenage Witch , The West Wing , ER , Grounded for Life , The Laramie Project , Married to the Kellys , Star Trek: Enterprise , Boston Legal , George Lopez , 7th Heaven , The Young and the Restless , Psych , Better Off Ted , The Client List , The Mindy Project , The Legend of Korra , Mom , Two and a Half Men , Black-ish , NCIS , The Middle and Another Period .

Riehle’s latest TV credits include American Housewife (2019) and Fuller House (2020). His last role was playing Warden Reynolds in HBO’s Barry (2023).

A woman has revealed that she complained to Channel 4 about Russell Brand’s behavior in 2009 after he allegedly put his head in her lap and demanded a massage, a court has heard.

The woman, whom we are calling Complainant 6 (C6) as she has a lifelong right to anonymity , was working for Channel 4 at the time of the alleged attack. Giving evidence as part of Brand’s rape trial, C6 claimed she reported her experience to her line manager and was assured the matter had been escalated.

Russell Brand Trial: Witnesses Say Their Friend Was "Extremely Distressed" After Alleged Anal Rape

Brand faces three charges of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one of indecent assault based on allegations made by six women . He will set out his defense later in the trial, denies all charges and has pleaded not guilty. Deadline has been reporting from a live video feed of the courtroom since the trial began, but a tech outage meant remote access was down this morning.

Watch on Deadline

In evidence to London’s Southwark Crown Court, C6 alleged that the comedian and actor had forced her to give him a massage. Speaking from behind a screen, she said she was working for Channel 4 at the time and had “briefly” met Brand once before. According to Sky News, C6 alleged Brand briefly left the room they were both in, returned and lay his head on her lap, before saying, “Come on then.”

C6 alleged she could feel his breath on her vagina. “I just thought I need to get him off me, so my hands went down at a diagonal [during the massage]. I was so repulsed by the situation I just thought, ‘Oh, you’re so bony. Ugh,” she was quoted by Sky News as telling the courtroom.

The court has been told repeatedly that Brand declined to answer questions when interviewed by police. He instead relied on a prepared statement, in which he claimed that he did not recall meeting the women and did not remember their names. He said any sexual contact was consensual.

Yesterday at the trial, a former MTV employee said she didn’t initially report her allegation of rape against Brand because she feared being “seen as trouble.”

The trial continues.

article_text:
Acclaimed British theater director Dominic Cooke , behind the recent stage spin-off “Game of Thrones: The Mad King,” is to helm his first film since 2020’s Benedict Cumberbatch-starring spy thriller “The Courier.”

“John Daniel,” which has been acquired for worldwide sales by Cornerstone ahead of the American Film Market, is based on the extraordinary true story of an unlikely friendship between a fiercely independent Englishwoman and a baby gorilla in the aftermath of WWI. With a screenplay written by Alexi Kaye Campbell (“Woman in Gold”), the film is inspired by original home movie footage and photographs recorded by locals in Uley, Gloucestershire between 1918-22.

Related Stories

‘Young Sheldon’ Star Iain Armitage Says the Show Was a ‘Big Undertaking’ as Co-Star Acknowledges He Could Be ‘Difficult’ to Work With

‘Young Sheldon’ Star Iain Armitage Says He Was the ‘Most Happy’ About the Show Ending: I Wasn’t ‘Going Home and Crying All Day’

“John Daniel” is a Genesius Pictures production, in association with Edward Film Company and produced by BAFTA nominee Debbie Gray (“Good Luck to You Leo Grande,” “Mrs Lowry & Son”). The film is currently in pre-production, with principal photography scheduled to begin in the U.K. in mid-2027. According to the filmmakers, motion capture and VFX will be used to “deliver a photoreal performance” of the gorilla, with visual effects by Axio World, led by Loris Mantello (“Avengers: Infinity War,” “Prehistoric Planet,” “The Lion King”) and Maoris Creantor (“The Lion King,” “Fast & Furious 9,” “The Matrix Resurrections”).

Set in 1918 in the Cotwolds village of Uley, still raw from the losses of WWII, “John Daniel” follows Alyce Cunningham, who has built a solitary life behind a wall of wit and stoicism. As per the synopsis, that changes when her reckless nephew impulsively rescues a baby gorilla from the window of a London department store and, ignoring her protests, leaves her no option but to take him in. Mischievous and endlessly curious, John Daniel, as she reluctantly names him, slowly wins her over, and as he becomes part of village life, from the school classroom to the village pub, he brings joy back to the grieving community. When fear and suspicion threaten to drive him out, Alyce must decide how far she will go to protect the animal who has opened her heart.

“The moment I read this beautiful script by Alexi, I knew I wanted to be part of it,” said Gray. “It’s an extraordinary true story about a gorilla, but at its heart it’s a story of love, hope and human connection in the aftermath of war. At a time when the world can feel increasingly divided, this film reminds us of our capacity to heal, unite and find compassion again.”

Added Cooke: “I am delighted to be attached to direct John Daniel – a beautiful, funny and profound story. Alexi’s script gets to the heart of the strange, necessary bonds between humans and animals. It shows how we sometimes need to surrender control in order to feel fully alive. I couldn’t be happier to be working with such committed and driven producers as Debbie Gray and the team at Cornerstone to bring this moving and hopeful true story to life.”

“John Daniel” marks the third feature from Cooke following “The Courier” and his 2017 directorial debut “On Chesil Beach,” based on Ian McEwan’s Booker Prize-nominated novella and starring Saoirse Ronan and Billy Howle.

Cooke is represented by UTA and Casarotto Ramsay & Associates.

article_text:
椎名林檎 党大会 令和八年列島巡回

劇場公開日： 2026年10月16日

解説・あらすじ

椎名林檎が2026年春に開催したライブツアー「椎名林檎 党大会 令和八年列島巡回」の模様を収録した映像作品をスクリーン上映。5月1日に東京・すみだトリフォニーホールで行われた公演を収録。 2026年3月から5月にかけて椎名林檎が敢行した「椎名林檎 党大会 令和八年列島巡回」。前回2013年の「党大会」は東京・神山町限定で開催されたが、今回は「列島巡回」のタイトルを冠し、音響に定評のある全国8カ所の会場で全18公演を実施した。ステージには、石若駿（ドラム）、鳥越啓介（ベース）、名越由貴夫（ギター）、林正樹（ピアノ、キーボード）ら近年のツアーやレコーディングを支えるバンドメンバーに加え、村田陽一（トロンボーン）、西村浩二（トランペット）、山本拓夫（テナーサックス、フルート）によるホーンセクション、さらに吉田宇宙（第1バイオリン）、名倉主（第2バイオリン）、奥田瑛生（ビオラ）、林田順平（チェロ）によるカルテットなど精鋭の演奏家たちが集結し、椎名林檎の歌唱とともに緻密かつダイナミックなアンサンブルを繰り広げた。 劇場上映では大きなスクリーンを通してステージ全体をとらえながら、映画館ならではの音響空間で臨場感たっぷりにライブを再現する。

2026年製作／115分／G／日本 配給：ライブ・ビューイング・ジャパン 劇場公開日：2026年10月16日

article_text:
A Revista ZUM e a Biblioteca de Fotografia do Instituto Moreira Salles anunciam os três livros premiados pela Convocatória de Fotolivros ZUM/IMS 2026.

Escola em casa: sentimentos presenciais (Mercúrio Editora), de Zélú , usa a fotografia para compartilhar experiências sensíveis vividas por estudantes secundaristas durante e após a pandemia de Covid-19, entre 2020 e 2025. Naquele momento em que o convívio escolar esteve comprometido, foi necessário refundar as formas de ensinar, criar, imaginar e manter vivo o elo comunitário. Em imagens que apresentam experiências educacionais, percorremos gestos que reinventam o arquivo escolar, fazendo dele não apenas um registro, mas também um espaço de afeto e sonhos, no qual salas de aula, pátios e corredores se tornam cenários de cumplicidade e formação constante.

Hay pájaros en el alambre (Hydra), da mexicana Gabriela García Rivas , entrelaça a memória de infância da autora à história das lutas indígenas e do movimento zapatista em Chiapas, no México. Fotografias produzidas por seus pais, médicos envolvidos na organização de sistemas comunitários de saúde, são revisitadas a partir de um olhar que oscila entre a experiência pessoal e a memória política. Com uma cuidadosa experimentação gráfica, que lança mão de diferentes papéis, texturas e técnicas de impressão, o livro transforma o arquivo familiar em testemunho de resistência e da construção coletiva de outras possibilidades de vida.

Em Talvez o nosso amor morra num sonho (Fotô Editorial), Caia Marvento Ramalho revê sua história em uma narrativa delicada e introspectiva. Da imersão no arquivo pessoal e familiar nasce uma operação que, longe do simples resgate nostálgico ou da celebração do álbum doméstico, funciona como um exercício de descontinuidade, reinterpretação e fabulação sobre a transição de gênero, a identidade e a trama afetiva. Intercalada a textos em primeira pessoa, a fotografia de amigos e família é tratada como um corpo estendido no tempo, em que as lacunas e silêncios contam tanto quanto aquilo que está visível.

Nas palavras do jurí, “os três premiados, de formatos e propostas distintos, combinam tempos diversos para refletir sobre educação, sociedade, corpo e relações de identidade. Entre memórias individuais e experiências coletivas, amplificam a potência dos fotolivros na construção de afetos, mundos possíveis e sonhos revolucionários”.

Cada um dos três escolhidos receberá um prêmio de R$ 2 mil. Este ano o júri foi composto por Aldeide Delgado (historiadora da arte e curadora), Luciara Ribeiro (historiadora da arte e curadora), Thyago Nogueira (coordenador do núcleo de arte contemporânea do IMS e editor da revista ZUM), Ângelo Manjabosco (pesquisador do IMS) e Miguel Del Castillo (coordenador da Biblioteca de Fotografia do IMS).

article_text:
A new Philippine-Italian sales alliance aims to put independent films in front of buyers in Asia, Europe and North America. Fire & Ice Media, the Philippine producer and sales agent, and Italy’s Coccinelle Film Sales unveiled the strategic partnership at Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market.

The pair will work together on a handpicked group of films, combining their regional know-how and buyer contacts to seek distribution deals beyond the films’ home markets. A first batch of films has already been chosen, though the companies have yet to name them.

Abell Diño-Cabrera, who heads Fire & Ice Media and runs the division’s film and TV development, production, positioning and sales work, will steer the alliance for the Philippine side.

“Every film has its own audience and its own potential in different markets. Our job is to understand where those opportunities are and work with the right people to make them happen,” said Diño-Cabrera. “Partnering with Coccinelle allows us to strengthen our reach, share market knowledge, and create more possibilities for the filmmakers and producers who trust us to represent their work.”

Coccinelle, set up by Francesca Breccia, sells independent titles on the international circuit, pairing films and their rights owners with buyers and distributors in a range of territories. Breccia said the company already had sales alliances with Asian counterparts, notably in South Korea and Thailand, and was delighted to now bring the Philippines into that network.

“Filipino cinema has a strong identity and remarkable creative energy, with stories and voices that deserve greater international exposure. I was particularly drawn to Fire & Ice Media’s lineup, which combines a distinctive arthouse sensibility with strong commercial potential,” Breccia said. “I look forward to joining forces and creating new opportunities for independent films across international markets.”

Fire & Ice was at the Asian Contents & Film Market with a slate of Filipino titles. On offer are Phil Giordano’s “Bilyarista,” a sports drama with a female lead; Nigel Santos’ queer ensemble piece “Open Endings”; David R. Corpuz’s “Only Known to Us”; Law Fajardo’s “The Hearing”; and “Crosspoint,” a Philippines-Japan thriller from Donie Ordiales. A selection of films by Brillante Mendoza rounds out the lineup.

Several international co-productions and development projects are also in the works. Among them are Mendoza’s “Aid,” Ham Tran’s supernatural thriller “Red Thread” and “Karaoke News,” a crime thriller from John Paul Su that takes aim at the media.

Parent company Fire & Ice Entertainment, co-founded by CEO Liza Diño and Ice Seguerra, spans film and TV production, international sales, music, live events and creative consultancy. Its Media arm has been a partner on international co-productions such as Nicole Midori Woodford’s “Last Shadow at First Light,” which bowed in San Sebastián in 2023, and Matsubayashi Urara’s “Blue Imagine,” a 2024 Rotterdam premiere.

The company’s homegrown projects include “Never the Bride,” a scripted drama series from Diño about a wedding planner whose own marriage is falling apart, and “Funeral Flowers,” a family drama feature she will write and direct. Seguerra is attached to direct “Alex & Rio,” a road movie driven by music.

Diño said the company had learned over the years that a robust slate is merely the starting point.

“Every market is different. Buyers have their own interests, audiences have different tastes, and sometimes a film finds its opportunity through a conversation with the right person who understands what it has to offer,” she said. “That’s what makes this collaboration with Coccinelle meaningful to us. We bring different strengths, relationships, and knowledge of our respective markets. But ultimately, we share the same goal: to serve the films we represent, find the right partners who believe in them, and give these stories the best possible opportunity to reach audiences. We see this as the beginning of a meaningful long-term relationship.”

article_text:
Note: This review was originally published as part of our 2026 Cannes coverage. The film arrives in theaters on November 13.

In 1858, pre-Freud times, a castle in the Yorkshire moors of Northern England by the name of Ensor House becomes the new dwelling place for young governess Winifred Notty (Maika Monroe, on a horror streak from Longlegs ). What awaits her is a predictably stilted family of huge wealth, the Pounds, comprising Mrs. Pounds (Ruth Wilson), Mr. Pounds (Jason Isaacs), the heir Andrew (Jacobi Jupe), and their teenage daughter Drusilla (Evie Templeton), but the script—based on Virginia Feito’s novel of the same name—has more than a few surprises in store for all. By following the erotic thriller Sanctuary with a period piece and a mysterious premise, director Zachary Wigon makes the most of this turn towards gothic horror: the delightfully wacky Victorian Psycho can be a testament to both his adaptability and commitment to genre.

Once in the manor house, Mrs. Notty (funnily homonymous to “naughty”) is tasked with educating the children on anything from table manners to family history, all the while bestowing a sense of her exemplary moral compass, at least in theory. At the same time, Winifred’s confessional voiceover pierces the film’s dramaturgy with sarcastic remarks that allude to her psychopathic tendencies, metaphorically winking at the audience. “My name is Winifred Notty and I’m the sanest person I’ve ever met,” she declares during the opening scene, evoking laughter and empathy––not least because the viewer is much more educated on the predicaments of Victorian women than these characters. Even though it’s not said out loud, Victorian Psycho agrees with the psychoanalytical provocation that hysteria and pathology are perhaps the only sane responses to an insane world.

Monroe’s face is framed in frequent close-ups and a slightly tilted angle to enlarge her ever-present, eerie smile, the camerawork of Nico Aguilar quite literally embodying the twisted inner workings of the main character’s mind. We’re talking canted angles, flipping the frame upside-down, and anxious, breathy camera movements that create a jarring sense of excitement. Victorian Psycho is aware of its debts to Brian De Palma and American Psycho while treating its female protagonist with a curiosity that’s not fetishistic. It also toes the line between identification and criticism very skillfully, employing a good amount of humor to diffuse any accusations of either. Mrs. Notty is also hilariously honest even as she admits to committing crimes or gives the children a lecture on evil. Even when she’s cruel enough to smash the head of an innocent animal to prove a point, her wackiness, à la Poor Things ‘ Bella Baxter, is hard to resist.

At the same time, Victorian Psycho deserves praise for not making an alluring character out of her: the script (like the novel) makes sure we and the rest of these characters are aware of her dark past early on. Still, she admits to “feeling tenderly” towards her darkness and externalizes it with an elegance unmatched in recent female-led horrors. Ariel Marx’s deviant score accompanies Winifred’s character on her descent towards madness—not only by incorporating the whispers and screams haunting her, but with the help of strings and dramatic arcs that accentuate the theatricality and delight she takes in every act of cruelty.

More than a well-crafted thriller, Victorian Psycho proves a rousing comedy, its trio of great actors never missing the mark with a stoic line delivery. Like Monroe, Wilson and Isaacs are a perfect match when they try to outperform each other’s ridiculousness without concealing, for even a second, how cold-hearted their characters are. An award for Best Inanimate Object Cameo should go to the pineapple (perhaps a throwback to that one line in Yorgos Lanthimos’ The Favourite ) happily acquired by young master Andrew, itself one of the film’s mildest jokes. Even if you don’t normally show that much appreciation for the kind of dark humor Victorian Psycho employs—slightly misandrist, at times anti-natalist, but always anti-classist—Wigon and his collaborators might convert you to that darker side, if only for the film’s duration.

Victorian Psycho premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.

article_text:
Prairie , a Chicago gallery that helped put a range of cutting-edge artists on the path to success, will close after nine years.

The gallery announced its closure on Friday by revealing that its forthcoming exhibition, a group show called “Retrospective,” would be its final one. “This will be our last show,” the gallery wrote on Instagram.

Founded in 2017 by Tim Mann and Jack Schneider as an artist-run space, the gallery had a name that referred to “the ecosystem that thrived in and around Chicago prior to the region’s colonization and industrialization,” per a description written for a prior edition of Chicago Exhibition Week. It sought to show art in a setting that was “free from the pressures of commercial viability.”

While many galleries have closed in response to the pressures of the art market, Schneider said Prairie’s shuttering had little to do with money.

“We were never a market-oriented space,” Schneider said on Monday. “I think an artist friend of ours, Mira Dayal, recently used the phrase ‘commercially irreverent’ to describe her practice, and I think that pretty perfectly describes our program and approach. We never expected to turn a profit, and we never did. We only ever, through occasional sales, fundraising, and occasional grants, raised just enough money to run the program itself.”

The shuttering had been planned for a year, Mann added, calling the occasion “a nice celebratory moment to close on.”

The gallery had a reputation for pinpointing noteworthy talents during the earliest stages of their careers.

Isabelle Frances McGuire, whose beguiling sculptures of witches struck a chord at the recent Whitney Biennial , had her first solo show ever with Prairie, in 2017. André Magaña, a standout of the 2026 edition of MoMA PS1’s Greater New York quinquennial , had his second-ever one-person exhibition with Prairie, in 2019.

Kira Scerbin, Craig Jun Li, Max Guy, Katz Tepper, ASMA, ektor garcia, and Amina Ross also showed with the gallery.

Mann said that Priairie was founded in his and Schneider’s studio with a tradition of edgy alternative spaces in mind. Drawing influence from Chicago outfits such as New Capital and Queer Thoughts (which later moved to New York and became influential there ), Prairie showcased a range of artists whose work might not have fit neatly into the commercial ecosystem. The relatively low cost of rent in Chicago helped, he added.

Schneider said that he and Mann planned to continue their work together. “We want to do curatorial work, just outside the guise of an artist-run space,” he noted.
